client: I've been really struggling since my dog passed away last month. He was with me for eleven years, and now everything just feels kind of hollow — like the things I used to enjoy don't really do anything for me anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help — and I'm really glad you did. Losing a companion of eleven years is a profound grief, and that hollowness you're describing, where things that once brought joy now feel flat, is such a natural response to that kind of loss. I'd love to understand a little more about what your days have felt like since he passed — are there particular moments or times of day that feel the heaviest for you?

client: Mornings are the worst, honestly. I used to wake up and he'd be right there at the foot of the bed, and now I just wake up to this silence that feels almost loud, if that makes any sense. I find myself reaching for my phone to check the time and then that split second of forgetting hits me, and then I remember, and it's like losing him all over again every single day.
therapist: That image of "loud silence" makes complete sense, and it's such a painfully honest way to describe grief — your whole morning routine was quietly built around him without you even realizing it. That moment of forgetting and then remembering is one of the cruelest parts of loss, like a small wound that reopens before you're even fully awake. I'm curious — in those moments after the remembering hits, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind?

client: It's usually something like... why didn't I call him more, or why did I waste that last visit talking about stupid stuff like the weather instead of actually saying something real. And then there's this awful feeling like I should have known somehow, like I should have sensed it was coming and done something differently. I know that's not rational, but in those half-awake moments it feels completely true.
therapist: What you're describing — that quiet, heavy self-blame — is incredibly common in grief, and the fact that you can already see it isn't fully rational shows real self-awareness, even if it doesn't make it hurt any less in those moments. Those thoughts are your mind's way of trying to find control in something that was ultimately uncontrollable, as if finding a "mistake" somehow means the loss could have been prevented. I'd gently ask you to consider — if a close friend came to you with those same thoughts after losing someone they loved, what do you think you would say to them?

client: I know what I'd say to a friend — I'd tell them it wasn't their fault, that they did the best they could. But when I try to turn that around on myself, it just feels... hollow, like I'm saying the words without believing them. It's different when it's you, you know? I can't just logic my way out of feeling like I should have visited more, called more, been there more.
therapist: That gap between knowing something and truly *feeling* it is one of the most frustrating parts of grief, and you're not alone in experiencing it — it doesn't mean the compassion you'd offer a friend is wrong, just that it hasn't found its way inward yet, and that takes time. What you're describing isn't a failure of logic, it's actually a sign of how deeply you loved him — the "should haves" are really just love with nowhere left to go. I wonder, when you think back over those eleven years, are there moments that come to mind where you *were* fully there for him — times that feel true to the kind of companion you actually were?

client: I like what you said about the "should haves" being love with nowhere left to go... that actually hit me somewhere real. But when I try to think of those moments where I was fully there for him, my mind just keeps pulling me back to the end, to those last few weeks when I was so exhausted and overwhelmed. It's like the good memories are there somewhere, but they're buried under all this weight.
therapist: I'm really glad that landed for you, and the fact that it did tells me part of you is ready to receive a little of that compassion, even if it's just a crack in the door right now. It's so common in grief for the painful recent memories to sit right at the surface, almost like they're standing guard over the warmer ones — but those good memories aren't gone, they're just waiting for some of that weight to lift. I'd love to try something gentle with you — if you let yourself go back to just one ordinary, unremarkable moment with him from those eleven years, something small and everyday, what's the first thing that comes to mind?

client: I close my eyes for a second and... there's this image of him just sitting at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning, reading the newspaper with his coffee, not saying much. It's so small, so nothing, but I can feel the warmth of it, like the whole house felt safe in that moment. I didn't realize how much I miss that quiet until just now, and it kind of catches me off guard how much it hurts.
therapist: That image is so beautiful, and the fact that it came to you so naturally tells me those memories are very much alive in you — that warmth hasn't gone anywhere. What you're feeling right now, that bittersweet ache, is actually grief and love existing in the same moment, and I think it's significant that a memory this tender surfaced when you gave yourself just a little space. I'm wondering — what does it feel like to sit with that image for a moment, knowing that the safety you felt in it was something real that you both shared?

client: It feels... I don't know, both comforting and painful at the same time, which is kind of confusing to me. Like, I want to hold onto that image but it also makes me feel this sharp loneliness because she's not here anymore and I can't just call her up and tell her I was thinking about her. I guess I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with that feeling — sitting with it sounds nice in theory, but it doesn't really make the loneliness go away, does it?
therapist: That bittersweet confusion makes complete sense — you're not doing it wrong, that's actually what love feels like when it has nowhere new to go, and it's okay for it to be both things at once. You're right that sitting with it doesn't make the loneliness disappear, and I'd never want to suggest it does — but what it can do over time is help the warmth and the pain coexist, so the memory of her feels less like a wound and more like something you get to keep. I also noticed you said "she" just now — it sounds like there's a real person woven into this grief too, and I want to make sure I'm understanding who you're carrying all of this for — can you tell me a little more about her?

client: Yeah, she was my grandmother. She passed about eight months ago, and I still catch myself thinking I should call her, like genuinely reaching for my phone before I remember. It's embarrassing to still be this raw about it, honestly, like I should be further along by now.
therapist: There is no "should be further along" in grief — the fact that you still reach for the phone is not a sign you're stuck, it's a sign she mattered deeply and was woven into the everyday fabric of your life. And there's nothing embarrassing about that rawness; losing your grandmother and your dog within months of each other is a real accumulation of loss, and your heart has been carrying a lot. I'm curious — where did that idea come from, that you should be past this by now, is that something you've heard from others or more of a voice from inside yourself?

client: I think it's mostly an internal voice, honestly. Like, I have this sense that I should be more functional by now, that other people deal with loss and keep going, and I'm somehow failing at it. Nobody's actually said that to me out loud, but I carry it around like it's a rule I'm supposed to be following.
therapist: That internal voice can be one of the hardest to push back against precisely because it feels like *your* voice, like it's just stating facts rather than telling a story. But I'd gently point out that you've just described losing two deeply loved companions within eight months — that's not a small thing to "keep going" through, and functioning through grief isn't the same as healing from it. Where do you think that rule came from — is there something in your history that taught you that needing time to grieve was a kind of weakness?

client: I think it probably came from my dad, honestly. He wasn't a cruel person, but whenever I was upset about something, he'd say things like "life goes on" or "you can't let things stop you" — and I guess I internalized that as the right way to be. It's strange to hear you say that functioning through grief isn't the same as healing, because part of me wants to argue with it, but another part of me feels something kind of... loosen, a little, when you put it that way.
therapist: That loosening you felt is worth paying attention to — it's your deeper self recognizing something true, even while the part shaped by your father's voice isn't quite ready to let go of the old rule. He likely taught you that lesson out of his own way of coping, maybe even out of love, but you're allowed to examine it now and decide if it actually serves you. I'm wondering — what might it look like for you to grieve in a way that felt true to *you*, rather than following a rule someone else handed you without even knowing it?
